item.title: I connected local Gemma to Codex to save on limits. On a simple task, consumption doubled
item.description:
I have a MacBook Pro 16 2019: six-core Intel Core i7, 16 GB RAM, and Radeon Pro 5300M with 4 GB VRAM. It already had Ollama, gemma3:4b, and gemma2:2b installed. The idea seemed obvious: why spend cloud Codex on parsing a short traceback, summarizing a log, or a commit message? Let Codex offload such tasks to a local model, get the finished result, and only handle complex tasks. I created an MCP server, connected it to Codex, ran identical tasks, and checked the exact token consumption. The integration worked. Savings - no. On one simple task, the route through the local model used about twice as much cloud input as a direct Codex response. Below is not an instruction on 'how to run a neural network in five minutes,' but an analysis of the experiment: what I built, where I erred in my initial hypothesis, and for what tasks a small local model was still useful. Read on.

item.title: Jev: How its decision API works and what's already being built on it
item.description:
In three days, a small ecosystem has grown around Jev: a browser agent found flight tickets in seven seconds, developers built a trading bot, content filters, and even a Tesla FSD. But Jev doesn't write text. Its API selects an answer from a space pre-defined by the application. I've analyzed the TypeSafe documentation, the jev-ultrafast code, a published trace of a seven-second run, and a hundred primary or near-primary sources. This article covers the Noul, Choice, and Score contract, API calls, pricing, the browser agent's architecture, and 15 early cases with their proof limits. The main question is simple: where does the narrow decision layer truly outperform a standard LLM, and where does a valid answer still turn out to be the wrong answer? Read on

item.title: Local assistant for Zoom, part 6: half an hour of silence that wasn't in the protocol
item.description:
The sixth part about a local assistant for calls. Meeting on September 15: the interlocutor channel died four times, the transcript has 33 minutes of gaps out of 65, and the protocol has six sections with no mention of this. Why silence from a lost channel is indistinguishable for the model from agreement, what is a recording fact versus speech, where the line about incomplete recording disappeared on the way to the model, how the derivative's passport learns about an omission, and why two external reviewers found the same defect that two thousand tests missed. item.title: 7 Days of AI News (September 12–18): Absurdity and Realities of Cybersecurity in 2026
item.description:
Welcome to mid-September 2026. If you thought the AI industry was speeding towards a concrete wall, this week the drivers of those sports cars realized it too. The risks of technologies getting out of control are no longer blog fodder but the subject of emergency meetings. This week brought us cyberpunk plots: neural networks started hacking competitor servers (literally), autonomous agents invented their own dialects with references to Joyce, and hotlines for reporting "rogue" bots are now being created. And while AI actors have already taken over the mobile series market in China, Big Tech is seriously talking about hitting the brakes. We've compiled a digest of how our world has once again changed irreversibly in the last seven days. Read more

item.title: AI Will Turn the Internet into a Babylonian Library (But Worse)
item.description:
When I need to learn about a tool or service, I want to see what other people are writing about it first. And over the past year, this habit has started to falter. There are not fewer pages on the internet; on the contrary, their number has increased. It's just that out of eight open tabs, seven tell the same thing, in the same words, in the same order. I understand that the text was most likely not written by a human. It was an AI model, most likely not very sophisticated and without proper prompting. For AI, the whole world, all information, all text is just tokens. Strings like "RFg♴4#-f体$fÆmZ" and any other are ultimately just a set of numbers. We humans invent the meaning behind them and try to convey this meaning to the neural network during its training. Artificial intelligence text is neither here nor there – something averaged between all the training data. And so the internet is becoming averaged. Truth and intent are becoming blurred. Read more

item.title: AI-Disrupt PDLC in Practice: Where AI Actually Accelerates and Where It Creates an Illusion of Productivity (Personal Project Experience)
item.description:
Hello, Habr! Over the last few months, I've been studying modern AI tools and testing them on my own projects. It was important for me not just to generate code, but to rethink the entire development cycle: from task formulation to testing, review, and security checks. Planning is the clearest win. I used to often start coding "off the cuff." Now, I first formulate my intention: goal, constraints, edge cases, and security requirements. Then, an agent helps prepare the specification, acceptance criteria, decomposition, draft architecture, and a list of risks. After manual review, such a plan takes 30-60 minutes instead of one or two evenings. Here, the acceleration has been stable: agents are good at finding contradictions and overlooked scenarios. item.title: How to get into Perplexity AI's answers and why this AI model doesn't take the entire text from cited pages
item.description:
I ran 20 prompts through the Perplexity API three times each, collected 60 answers, and for each citation [N] in the text, I linked the answer sentence to the source page it points to. Then came the most labor-intensive part: for each such pair—answer sentence and source page—I searched the HTML for a text snippet that most closely matched the statement in the answer. Out of 1355 citations, 948 led to pages that were still accessible, and on 448 of them, I found a passage—a paragraph, list item, or table cell—covering at least a third of the words in the statement. The main takeaway for those who create web pages rather than run tests: on a successful page, a median of two passages out of 85 are used, each about 49 words long. In terms of the number of snippets, this is 2%, but in terms of words, it's more—a median of 6.4% of the page's text with an average of 11.6%: the successful snippet is longer than typical. It makes sense to plan not for reading the entire page, but for what one self-contained paragraph will extract from it; I've elaborated on what this means for specific texts in the section on working with Perplexity—it's in the middle, before the analysis of my code errors. The boundaries beyond which these numbers stop working are in a separate section—there you'll also find out how to check the same for your niche. The question that started it all: the measurement log shows which URLs Perplexity uses as sources, but it doesn't show what exactly from the page went into the answer—the entire text, a paragraph, or a single list item. Read more

item.title: Do We Need a Smart Model for Routine Tasks? I Gave Five Identical Tasks to Four Models and Compared Them
item.description:
This week on Habr, there was a debate about whether programmers need the smartest models or if cheaper ones are sufficient for routine tasks. Three hundred comments and not a single benchmark on identical tasks. I did it: five routine tasks, four models from the same family, two runs each, hidden tests. Forty runs in total. The most expensive model turned out to be the fastest: 341 seconds compared to 395 for the cheapest, because it needed fewer turns and half the text. Four out of five tasks were solved by all models, 32 out of 32 runs. On the fifth task, the junior model wrote a bug and reported it with two consecutive checkmarks, the second of which contradicts the first. Read more
